searchText: > BTW <@!301186049323958275> <@!273808422753796097> Is there any rationale behind the symmetry between increase and decrease for the change denominator ? i.e Would the security be affected if we had a different max change denominator on both sides. For example 1/8 on the increase side and 1/4 on the decrease side. That would allow 33% of miners to push the basefee down to zero It's only symmetry and the 2x limit that keep the threshold for all of the different attacks at ~50% Hmm, really? I thought the percentage required was a function of elasticity, not the base fee change rate? Ah, I suppose that assumes symmetry. The percentage required definitely also depends on the cost/risk curve of higher block sizes 🤔 that means we can actually use asymmetry the other direction to increase the hashing power required to attack. But from a mon-manipulability point of view, 2x is best Asymmetry in the other direction (eg. 1/8 down, 1/4 up) would allow 1/3 to push the fee upward I suppose it would be expensive for them to, but still.... 2x elastic blocks where base fee rises faster than it falls. well there's always a 51% censorship attack, so trying to be more than 51% secure doesn't really make sense I don't think there is *any* financial motive (outside of "burn Ethereum to the ground and profit off shorts") to pushing the base fee up though? right, that's fair, so limit = 3x target should be safe too I would not go above 3x Also, another important non-manipulability criterion is that the net effect of transactions on the basefee should not depend on which blocks the transactions are included in ie. [5, 15, 5] million gas and [20, 4, 1] million gas should lead to the same final gasprice Technically the current formula actually does not *quite* satisfy it Is there a formula that does guarantee that? And is it not terribly complicated? 😬 An ideally well-designed EIP 1559 would use exponential adjustment: `new_basefee = old_basefee * e ** ((gas_used - target) / k)` The current formula (linear) is within a few percent So it's close Ewe, irrational numbers are the worst. A quadratic Taylor approximation actually comes really really close to the ideal: `new_basefee = old_basefee + old_basefee * (gas_used - target) // (target * k) + old_basefee * (gas_used - target) ** 2 // (2 * (target * k) ** 2)` Heh, better than `e` I suppose. 😛 I wouldn't be opposed to switching to that if we think the gains are worth it. I do like the simplicity of the current algorithm though, it is easier to grok *why* it is what it is. > Also, another important non-manipulability criterion is that the net effect of transactions on the basefee should not depend on which blocks the transactions are included in <@!574864862338088960> This convinces me that symmetry is important. Our existing formula is already the 1st degree Taylor approximation and it's within a few percent of optimality We're technically 46.8% attackable (or somewhere around that) instead of 50% attackable, because it takes a little bit more than one full block to reverse the decrease from an empty block As (7/8) * (9/8) = 63/64 < 1 But meh, ethereum itself is actually attackable at around that same threshold due to uncles **EIP-1559 Implementers' Call #6 in ~45 minutes (16:00 UTC)** Agenda: https://github.com/ethereum/pm/issues/215 Zoom: https://consensys.zoom.us/j/92426301194 <@!574864862338088960> Nethermind is in sync with BeSu let me switch the validator on again 🥳 sealing blocks <@!489256758989029405> surprisingly since you joined i am not able to reach anymore ~200% block elasticity not urgent but we should investigate at some point https://hardhat.org/
